implementation_notes: In a Sidekiq deployment the control bus is the process signal protocol plus the Sidekiq API. Operationally the signals are the commands: TSTP quiets a process (stop fetching new jobs, finish the current ones), TERM requests shutdown within the -t timeout and pushes unfinished jobs back to Redis, TTIN dumps thread backtraces for a stuck worker. Where signals are unavailable (JRuby, Windows, Heroku), Sidekiq::ProcessSet#each(&:quiet!) / :stop! / :dump_threads are the same commands delivered over Redis - literally a message-based control bus - and the Web UI is a console built exclusively on that API. Queue-level operations (Sidekiq::Queue#clear, pause in Sidekiq Pro) and Stats/WorkSet provide the status half.
code_sketch:
require 'sidekiq/api'

Sidekiq::ProcessSet.new.each(&:quiet!)        # == TSTP: stop fetching, finish in-flight jobs
Sidekiq::ProcessSet.new.each(&:stop!)         # == TERM: graceful shutdown within -t timeout
Sidekiq::ProcessSet.new.each(&:dump_threads) if stuck?

Sidekiq::Stats.new.failed                     # status half: counters, queue depths, latency
Sidekiq::Queue.new('mailer').latency
pitfalls: The Sidekiq API reads and mutates Redis structures without locks: its results are best-effort snapshots, so a console must not treat counts or the process set as consistent and must not bulk-delete across a live system.

quiet!/stop! act on the process, not on individual jobs: a long-running job still delays shutdown until the timeout, after which it is forcefully terminated and re-enqueued - jobs must be idempotent for that to be safe.
Signals and the API can disagree (a process may have exited between the ProcessSet read and the command), so scripts should re-read state after acting instead of assuming the command landed.

variants.name: Signal.trap handlers plus ActiveSupport::Notifications instrumentation
variants.implementation_notes: Without Sidekiq (a plain Rack app or daemon), the control bus is Ruby's signal facility plus an instrumentation bus: Signal.trap('HUP') for reconfiguration, 'USR1' for an ad-hoc dump, 'TERM' for a controlled shutdown, with the trap block only setting a flag so the real work happens in the main loop. The status half in Rails is ActiveSupport::Notifications: instrument('integration.process') around a unit of work publishes an event (name, timing, payload, allocations) to subscribers, so a monitor subscribes instead of polling internals - the same shape as a control bus, with events flowing the other way. Use the Sidekiq variant when worker lifecycle, not application instrumentation, is what must be controlled.
variants.code_sketch:
Signal.trap('HUP')  { RELOAD = true }        # traps run asynchronously: set flags only
Signal.trap('TERM') { SHUTDOWN = true }

ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe('integration.process') do |event|
  metrics.record(event.name, event.duration, event.payload)      # status half
end

ActiveSupport::Notifications.instrument('integration.process', queue: 'orders') do
  handle_message
end
pitfalls: Signal.trap handlers run in a restricted context where most Mutex/Thread operations are unsafe, and they replace Ruby's default handler: heavy or blocking work in a trap is a hang, and the handler must tolerate a signal arriving during its own reload.

ActiveSupport::Notifications subscribers are synchronous and unguarded: an exception in a subscriber is re-raised into the instrumented business code (InstrumentationSubscriberError), so monitoring must never be able to break the flow it observes.
Flags set by traps are read at loop boundaries: a loop that blocks for minutes ignores the shutdown flag and looks unresponsive to the operator.
